processing: Sold under the Darjeeling name, with orthodox making typical of the region. Oxidation depends on the flush.
harvest_season: First flush lots are sold under this name; the slow growth of high gardens is typical, and later flushes follow as elsewhere in the district.
appearance_dry: Typically green-tinged olive leaf with pale tips in first flush lots.
appearance_wet: Bright green and light copper leaf in spring lots.
taste_profile: Little is reliably recorded about this cup. Typical of high first flush Darjeeling, expect a light, floral and brisk tea.

brewing.notes: Treat first flush lots gently: cooler water, shorter steeps, plenty of room for the leaf.

vintage_note: Usually met as a first flush of a stated year, spelled in several ways. Like other spring Darjeelings it is best drunk within about a year.
description:
Samabeong, also written Samabiyong and Samaebong, is a garden on hill slopes about 8 km from Lava, in today's Kalimpong district. It sits at roughly 2,000 metres, high for this part of the hills, and sometimes gets called the world's highest tea garden, a claim worth taking lightly.

High gardens typically grow slowly in cool weather, which is the usual explanation for fine spring tea from such places. The specific way this garden works is not well documented.

As with other high first flush teas, expect something light, floral and brisk. Brew it cool and short, because spring leaf from the hills turns sharp quickly.

The spellings are the main buying problem, so check several when searching. A first flush with a stated year is the usual form, and it should smell fresh when opened.
history: British planters established the garden in the 1880s; 1887 is the year most often repeated in reference accounts, while some tea sellers give 1882. Little else about how it developed is documented with confidence.
